title: Cleaning Noisy Labels Without a Clean Set or a Noise Rate: Out-of-Fold Disagreement Filtering for Linear Classifiers
insight: A linear classifier can find most of its own mislabeled training samples by checking which labels it cannot predict from the other folds, so label noise can be removed with no clean validation set and no noise-rate estimate.
abstract_sketch: Methods that defend against label noise usually need a clean validation set, an estimate of the noise rate, or a deep network, which a practitioner with a small tabular or image dataset often lacks. We show that a linear classifier can clean its own training set: fit logistic regression with 5-fold cross-validation, drop every sample whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with its given label, and refit on the rest. The reason it works is that a sample the other folds cannot explain is more likely mislabeled than one they explain. On two small datasets with symmetric noise up to 40%, the filter recovers a large share of the accuracy that noise costs logistic regression, most of what it drops is truly mislabeled, and it beats an untuned MLP trained on the same noisy labels. On clean labels it gives up a fraction of a point. The study is small and linear, and we make no claim about deep networks or large data.
figure1: One figure, three panels with numbered circles. Panel 1 (Noisy training set): a grid of digit thumbnails where flipped labels are marked with a red outline, labeled 'given labels' and 'no clean set, no noise rate'. Panel 2 (Out-of-fold check): five folds drawn as colored blocks, each predicted by a model fit on the other four; samples whose prediction disagrees with their label are crossed out and labeled 'disagree: drop'; a small counter shows that most crossed-out samples are the red-outlined ones (drop precision). Panel 3 (Refit and compare): grouped bars for digits and breast cancer at 40% noise: plain logistic regression, MLP, filter (Northwestern purple), and a gray clean-label reference (logistic regression at 0% noise), with error bars (sd over 5 seeds) and seed points. The reader sees the cleaning step, and that the filtered linear model sits above both the unfiltered model and the MLP. The bars are means over all seeds, and any thumbnails are drawn by a rule fixed before looking, stated in the caption.
contributions: We present an out-of-fold disagreement filter that lets a linear classifier remove its own noisy labels, using no clean validation set and no noise-rate estimate.

We show on two small datasets that the filter recovers much of the accuracy lost to symmetric label noise, drops mostly mislabeled samples, and beats an untuned MLP trained on the same noisy labels, with its gain growing with the noise rate on digits.
We report where it does not help: a small, statistically undetectable cost on clean labels, a weaker and unstable result on breast cancer at 40% noise, and about five times the fit time.
storyline: Practitioners with a noisy labeled set and a simple model rarely have a clean validation set or a reliable noise rate, and the standard noisy-label defenses assume one or the other, or a deep network. We make a capability available to this simple case: a linear classifier cleans its own training set by dropping every sample whose label it cannot predict from the other folds, then refits. The reason is that an out-of-fold prediction never saw the sample, so a disagreement is evidence the label is wrong, and it needs no external signal. Under symmetric noise the filter recovers most of the lost accuracy on digits and at 20% noise on both datasets, drops samples that are mostly truly mislabeled, and beats an MLP trained on the same labels, whose accuracy collapses under noise. The price is small and shown honestly: a fraction of a point on clean labels, an instability on breast cancer at 40% noise, and extra fit time. This makes a plain, checkable noise filter a sensible default step for linear models, and it frames the open question of how far the same check goes with other noise types, tuned models, and larger data.

sections.title: Label noise costs a linear model many points, and the filter wins most of them back
Most of what the filter drops is truly mislabeled
A filtered linear model beats an untuned MLP under noise
On clean labels the filter costs a fraction of a point

risks: A reviewer will say the capability is not new (confident learning also uses out-of-fold predictions), that two small sklearn datasets and five seeds prove little, and that an untuned MLP is a weak comparator. We answer by stating plainly what is and is not new (a simple, checkable filter for the linear case, with no noise rate used in the code), scoping every claim to digits, breast cancer, symmetric noise and a linear base, making no claim about deep networks or scale, and calling the MLP result a comparison with an untuned 64-unit MLP. We report paired tests and confidence intervals, show the weak cells (breast cancer at 20% noise not significant, at 40% unstable, only about 22% of the loss recovered), report the clean-label cost and fit-time overhead, and do not claim that 5 seeds prove equivalence on clean labels. Co-teaching and confident learning are not run as baselines, and the paper says so.
